prompt: Which statement gives the Arrhenius definitions of an acid and a base?

choices.text: An acid increases the amount of H+ in an aqueous solution; a base increases the amount of OH−
An acid increases the amount of OH− in an aqueous solution; a base increases the amount of H+
choices.why: The definitions are reversed. An acid increases H+, and a base, its chemical opposite, increases OH−.

choices.text: An acid is any compound that contains hydrogen; a base is any compound that contains oxygen
choices.why: Containing H or O doesn't decide it. H2SO4 contains both hydrogen and oxygen, but it is an acid because it increases the amount of H+ in water.

choices.text: An acid increases the amount of H+ in an aqueous solution; a base is any ionic compound that dissolves
choices.why: The acid half is right, but many ionic compounds that dissolve, such as NaCl, are not bases. A base must increase the amount of OH−.

explanation: Arrhenius defined an acid as a compound that increases the amount of hydrogen ion, H+, in an aqueous solution, and a base as a compound that increases the amount of hydroxide ion, OH−.

prompt: Which of these compounds is a base, as this section defines bases?

choices.why: H3PO4 contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms but no hydroxide ions. It increases the amount of H+ in water, so it is an acid.
RbCl has the same metal as RbOH, but its anion is Cl−, not OH−. It is the salt that forms when RbOH reacts with HCl.
KNO3 is made of K+ and NO3− ions and adds no OH− to water. It is the salt that forms when KOH reacts with HNO3.

explanation: A base increases the amount of OH− in an aqueous solution. RbOH is made of Rb+ and OH− ions, so dissolving it adds hydroxide ions to the water.

prompt: As this section defines bases, how many of these compounds are bases: KOH, H2SO4, Ba(OH)2, NaNO3, HC2H3O2, LiOH?
explanation: KOH, Ba(OH)2, and LiOH contain hydroxide ions and increase the amount of OH− in water, so they are bases. H2SO4 and HC2H3O2 increase H+ and are acids, and NaNO3 is a salt.

prompt: What is an H+ ion?

choices.text: A hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron, leaving just a proton
A hydrogen atom that has gained one extra electron
choices.why: Gaining a negative electron would make a negative ion. H+ is positive because the hydrogen atom has lost its electron.

choices.text: A hydrogen atom that has lost its proton, leaving just an electron
choices.why: An atom left with only its electron would not be a positive ion. H+ keeps its proton and loses its negative electron.

choices.text: A hydrogen molecule, H2, that has lost one of its electrons
choices.why: H+ comes from a single hydrogen atom, not an H2 molecule. A hydrogen atom has one electron, and losing it leaves a bare proton.

explanation: A hydrogen atom has one proton and one electron. An H+ ion is a hydrogen atom that has lost its lone electron, so H+ is simply a proton.

prompt: Written in terms of the hydronium ion, the net ionic equation for the reaction of HCl(aq) with NaOH(aq) is H3O+(aq) + OH−(aq) → 2H2O(ℓ). Why are there two water molecules on the product side?

choices.text: H3O+ is an H+ ion attached to a water molecule, and that water molecule ends up as a product
The OH− ion breaks apart and forms a second water molecule by itself
choices.why: OH− has only one oxygen atom, so it can end up in only one water molecule. The second one is the water molecule that carried the H+ in H3O+.

choices.text: The hydronium ion has a 2+ charge, so two water molecules are needed to balance it
choices.why: Hydronium has a 1+ charge, H3O+. The 2 balances atoms: the 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms on the left make two water molecules.

choices.text: This form describes a different reaction, one that produces more water than the H+ form
choices.why: The section says the two forms of the net ionic equation are equivalent, except for the extra water molecule that H3O+ brings with it.

explanation: Hydronium, H3O+, is an additional proton attached to a water molecule. The H+ and OH− combine to make one water molecule, and the water molecule that carried the H+ is the second one.

prompt: What are the products when an acid reacts with a base in a neutralization reaction?

choices.why: Hydrogen gas forms when an acid reacts with certain metals, as in a single-replacement reaction. An acid and a base produce water and a salt.
CO2 and H2O are the usual products of a fuel burning in oxygen, a combustion reaction. An acid and a base produce water and a salt.

choices.text: A new acid and a new base
choices.why: The acid and base cancel each other's chemistry, so neither an acid nor a base is produced. The products are water and a salt.

explanation: The general neutralization reaction is acid + base → water + salt. For example, HCl + KOH → H2O + KCl, where KCl is the salt.

prompt: In chemistry, what does the word salt mean?

choices.text: Any ionic compound formed when an acid reacts with a base
Only sodium chloride, the compound known as table salt
choices.why: In chemistry, salt refers to more than just table salt. KCl, MgCl2, and many other ionic compounds formed in neutralization reactions are salts.

choices.text: Only an ionic compound that dissolves in water
choices.why: A salt can be soluble or insoluble. What makes it a salt is that it is an ionic compound formed from an acid and a base.

choices.text: Any compound that increases the amount of H+ or OH− in water
choices.why: Increasing H+ or OH− in water is what acids and bases do. A salt is the ionic compound that forms when they react.

explanation: The section uses salt for any ionic compound, soluble or insoluble, that is formed from a reaction between an acid and a base. Table salt, NaCl, is just one example.

prompt: Which equation represents a neutralization reaction?

choices.why: An acid reacts here, but with a metal element, not a base. Zinc replaces the hydrogen, so this is a single-replacement reaction.
Two ionic compounds exchange ions and AgBr precipitates. Neither reactant is an acid or a base.
Water is a product, but this is methane burning in oxygen, a combustion reaction. A neutralization needs an acid and a base as reactants.

explanation: In a neutralization reaction, an acid reacts with a base to form water and a salt. HI is an acid and LiOH is a base, and they form H2O and the salt LiI.

prompt: When you balance a neutralization equation, what does the coefficient of H2O equal?

choices.text: It equals the total number of H+ ions the acid supplies, which matches the OH− ions the base supplies
It is always 1, because each neutralization reaction makes a single water molecule
choices.why: The number of water molecules depends on the reactants. In 2HNO3 + Ba(OH)2 → 2H2O + Ba(NO3)2, two water molecules form.

choices.text: It always equals the coefficient of the acid, because each acid molecule makes one water molecule
choices.why: That works only when each acid molecule supplies one H+. In H2SO4 + 2LiOH → 2H2O + Li2SO4, one H2SO4 makes two water molecules.

choices.text: It always equals the coefficient of the salt, because water and salt form in equal numbers
choices.why: In 3HCl + Fe(OH)3 → 3H2O + FeCl3, one FeCl3 forms along with three water molecules.

explanation: Each H+ from the acid combines with one OH− from the base to make one H2O. So the number of water molecules equals the number of H+ ions the acid supplies, which must match the number of OH− ions from the base.

prompt: In a neutralization reaction, which ions make up the salt?

choices.text: The cation from the base and the anion from the acid
The H+ from the acid and the cation from the base
choices.why: These are both positive ions. An ionic compound needs a cation and an anion, and the H+ from the acid goes into forming water.

choices.text: The anion from the acid and the OH− from the base
choices.why: These are both negative ions. An ionic compound needs a cation and an anion, and the OH− from the base goes into forming water.

choices.text: The H+ from the acid and the OH− from the base
choices.why: H+ and OH− combine to form water, the other product. The salt is made of the ions that are left: the base's cation and the acid's anion.

explanation: The acid's H+ and the base's OH− combine to form water. The remaining ions, the cation from the base and the anion from the acid, make up the salt; in HCl + KOH → H2O + KCl, K+ and Cl− form KCl.

prompt: Hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq), is neutralized by barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)2(aq). What is the name of the salt that forms?

choices.why: The hydro- prefix belongs only to the name of the acid. In the salt, Cl− is simply the chloride ion.
Ionic compounds are named without numerical prefixes, even though BaCl2 contains two chloride ions.
Chlorate is ClO3−, the anion of chloric acid. Hydrochloric acid contains no oxygen, so its anion is chloride, Cl−.

explanation: The salt is made of Ba^2+ and Cl− ions, BaCl2, and it is named like any ionic compound: barium chloride. The balanced equation is 2HCl(aq) + Ba(OH)2(aq) → 2H2O(ℓ) + BaCl2(aq).

prompt: Sulfurous acid is completely neutralized by potassium hydroxide, KOH. What is the formula of the salt that forms?

choices.why: SO4^2− is sulfate, the anion of sulfuric acid. Sulfurous acid, H2SO3, contains the sulfite ion, SO3^2−.
One K+ can't balance the 2− charge of the sulfite ion. Two K+ ions are needed for each SO3^2−.
The sulfite ion stays together as SO3^2−. The salt keeps the whole anion from the acid, not just the sulfur.

explanation: Sulfurous acid is H2SO3, made of H+ ions and the sulfite ion, SO3^2−. In the salt, two K+ ions balance the 2− charge of one sulfite ion: K2SO3, potassium sulfite.

prompt: Which acid and base react in a neutralization reaction to form iron(III) nitrate?

choices.why: Fe(OH)2 contains Fe^2+ and would form iron(II) nitrate. The (III) means the salt contains Fe^3+, which comes from Fe(OH)3.
HNO2 is nitrous acid, whose anion is nitrite, NO2−. A nitrate salt comes from nitric acid, HNO3.
FeCl3 contains no OH− ions, so it is not a base; it is itself a salt. The iron(III) must come from a base, Fe(OH)3.

explanation: Iron(III) nitrate, Fe(NO3)3, is made of Fe^3+ and NO3− ions. Nitric acid, HNO3, supplies the nitrate and iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)3, supplies the Fe^3+: 3HNO3 + Fe(OH)3 → 3H2O + Fe(NO3)3.

prompt: Some sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH(aq), spills on a lab bench. Which of these substances could neutralize it?

choices.why: Sr(OH)2 is also a base, since it increases the amount of OH− in water. A base is neutralized by an acid, not by another base.
Na2SO4 contains the anion of sulfuric acid, but it is a salt, the product of neutralizing H2SO4 with NaOH. It adds no H+, so it can't neutralize a base.
NaCl is a salt, the kind of compound a neutralization produces. It adds neither H+ nor OH− to water, so it can't neutralize a base.

explanation: NaOH is a base, so it is neutralized by an acid. Citric acid, the acid in citrus fruits, increases the amount of H+ in water, and that H+ reacts with the OH− from NaOH to form water.

prompt: Oxalic acid, H2C2O4(aq), is completely neutralized by sodium hydroxide, NaOH(aq). Which equation for this reaction is correct?

choices.why: The equation is balanced, but all compounds of Na+ are soluble, so sodium oxalate dissolves and is labeled (aq).
Two H+ ions react with two OH− ions, so two water molecules form. With only one H2O, the hydrogen and oxygen atoms don't balance.
The oxalate ion, C2O4^2−, needs two Na+ ions, so the salt is Na2C2O4. The hydrogen atoms in this equation don't balance either.

explanation: The salt pairs Na+ with the oxalate ion, C2O4^2−, giving Na2C2O4, which is soluble because all sodium compounds are. Two H+ and two OH− make two water molecules: H2C2O4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → 2H2O(ℓ) + Na2C2O4(aq).

prompt: A student writes the neutralization of chloric acid by zinc hydroxide as HClO3 + Zn(OH)2 → H2O + ZnClO3. What is the mistake?

choices.text: Zn^2+ needs two ClO3− ions, so the salt is Zn(ClO3)2, and the equation needs 2HClO3 and 2H2O
Zn(OH)2 doesn't dissolve in water, so no neutralization reaction can take place at all
choices.why: Neutralization reactions proceed even if one reactant is not in the aqueous phase, so the solid base still reacts with the acid.

choices.text: The products should be hydrogen gas and ZnClO3, since an acid reacts to give off hydrogen
choices.why: Hydrogen gas forms when an acid reacts with certain metals, not with a base. An acid and a base form water and a salt, and ZnClO3 still has unbalanced charges.

choices.text: The salt formula is right, and the equation only needs a coefficient of 2 in front of H2O
choices.why: ZnClO3 doesn't balance charges: Zn^2+ is 2+ and ClO3− is only 1−. A 2 in front of H2O alone wouldn't balance the hydrogen atoms either.

explanation: Zinc forms Zn^2+ and chlorate is ClO3−, so two chlorate ions are needed: Zn(ClO3)2. Two HClO3 supply the two ClO3− and two H+, which meet the two OH− to make two water molecules: 2HClO3 + Zn(OH)2 → 2H2O + Zn(ClO3)2.

prompt: Phosphoric acid, H3PO4(aq), is completely neutralized by sodium hydroxide, NaOH(aq). Balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of NaOH?
explanation: Each H3PO4 supplies three H+ ions, so three OH− ions are needed, and the salt is Na3PO4: H3PO4 + 3NaOH → 3H2O + Na3PO4.

prompt: Acetic acid, HC2H3O2(aq), is neutralized by barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)2(aq). Balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of H2O?
explanation: Only the first H in HC2H3O2 is an H+ ion; the other three are part of the acetate ion, C2H3O2−. Ba^2+ needs two acetate ions, so two HC2H3O2 react and two water molecules form: 2HC2H3O2 + Ba(OH)2 → 2H2O + Ba(C2H3O2)2.

prompt: Sulfuric acid, H2SO4(aq), neutralizes solid aluminum hydroxide, Al(OH)3(s). Predict the products and balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of H2O?
explanation: Al^3+ and SO4^2− make the salt Al2(SO4)3. Its two Al need 2Al(OH)3, which supply 6 OH−, and its three SO4^2− need 3H2SO4, which supply 6 H+; together they make 6H2O: 3H2SO4 + 2Al(OH)3 → 6H2O + Al2(SO4)3.

prompt: Phosphoric acid, H3PO4(aq), reacts with solid iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)3(s), in a neutralization reaction. Predict the products and balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the sum of all the coefficients, counting any coefficient of 1?
explanation: Fe^3+ and PO4^3− have charges of the same size, so the salt is FePO4. The three H+ from one H3PO4 meet the three OH− from one Fe(OH)3 to make three H2O: H3PO4 + Fe(OH)3 → 3H2O + FePO4, and 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 6.

prompt: Some antacids contain magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, and others contain aluminum hydroxide, Al(OH)3. Comparing one Mg(OH)2 with one Al(OH)3, which neutralizes more molecules of stomach acid, HCl?

choices.why: One Mg(OH)2 does neutralize two HCl, but one Al(OH)3 supplies three OH− ions and neutralizes three.
The number of HCl depends on the number of OH− ions, not on the single aluminum ion. Al(OH)3 has three OH− ions.
Each OH− reacts with one H+, so a base with more OH− ions neutralizes more HCl.

explanation: Each OH− reacts with one H+ from HCl. Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl → 2H2O + MgCl2, but Al(OH)3 + 3HCl → 3H2O + AlCl3, so one Al(OH)3 neutralizes three HCl and one Mg(OH)2 only two.

prompt: Rust contains iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)3(s), which does not dissolve in water. Why do some cleaning solutions for rust stains contain an acid?

choices.text: The acid neutralizes the Fe(OH)3, making products that are soluble and wash away
The acid turns the Fe(OH)3 into iron metal and hydrogen gas, which float away
choices.why: An acid reacting with a base produces water and a salt, not a metal and hydrogen gas.

choices.text: The acid turns the rust into an insoluble salt that can then be scraped off
choices.why: The salt that forms, such as FeCl3 with hydrochloric acid, is soluble. That is why the stain washes away.

choices.text: The acid dissolves the Fe(OH)3 without reacting, the way water dissolves sugar
choices.why: Fe(OH)3 is insoluble, so it doesn't just dissolve. The acid reacts with it in a neutralization, which proceeds even though Fe(OH)3 is a solid.

explanation: Fe(OH)3 is a base, and neutralization reactions proceed even when one reactant is not dissolved. With hydrochloric acid, 3HCl(aq) + Fe(OH)3(s) → 3H2O(ℓ) + FeCl3(aq), and the soluble products wash away.

prompt: Hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq), neutralizes solid nickel(II) hydroxide, Ni(OH)2(s). Which correctly shows the products of the balanced equation, with phase labels?

choices.why: Ni(OH)2 is insoluble, but the salt NiCl2 is soluble: chlorides are soluble except those of Ag+, Hg2^2+, and Pb^2+.
Water forms as a liquid and is written H2O(ℓ), as in every neutralization equation in the section.
Ni^2+ needs two Cl− ions, so the salt is NiCl2, and the two OH− ions in Ni(OH)2 make two water molecules.

explanation: Ni^2+ pairs with two Cl− ions to make NiCl2, which is soluble because chlorides are soluble except with Ag+, Hg2^2+, and Pb^2+. The balanced equation is 2HCl(aq) + Ni(OH)2(s) → 2H2O(ℓ) + NiCl2(aq).

prompt: Hydriodic acid neutralizes strontium hydroxide: 2HI(aq) + Sr(OH)2(aq) → 2H2O(ℓ) + SrI2(aq). In the complete ionic equation, how many ions in total are written on the reactant side? Count each ion separately, so 2I− counts as two ions.
explanation: Both reactants are dissolved, so they are written as separate ions: 2H+(aq) + 2I−(aq) + Sr^2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq). That is 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7 ions.

prompt: Which two neutralization reactions have the same net ionic equation?

choices.why: Zn(OH)2 is insoluble, so it stays together as a solid in its net ionic equation, which also produces Zn^2+(aq). The KOH reaction has no solid.
Fe(OH)2 is insoluble, so its net ionic equation keeps Fe(OH)2(s) and produces Fe^2+(aq). The Ba(OH)2 reaction has no solid.
Both bases are solids, but different ones, so the net ionic equations differ: one has Zn(OH)2(s) and Zn^2+, the other Fe(OH)2(s) and Fe^2+.

explanation: When the acid, base, and salt are all dissolved, the base's cation and the acid's anion are spectator ions, and the net ionic equation is H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(ℓ). KOH and Ba(OH)2 are soluble, so both of those reactions reduce to it; an insoluble base stays in its net ionic equation as a solid.

prompt: Nitric acid, HNO3(aq), reacts with solid copper(II) hydroxide, Cu(OH)2(s), to form water and copper(II) nitrate. Which ions are spectator ions in this reaction?

choices.why: Cu^2+ starts as part of the solid Cu(OH)2 and ends as a dissolved ion, so it changes form and is not a spectator.
H+ combines with OH− to form water, so it takes part in the reaction.
NO3− is dissolved on both sides of the complete ionic equation and does not change, so it is a spectator ion.

explanation: Copper(II) nitrate is soluble, but Cu(OH)2 is not, so the complete ionic equation is 2H+(aq) + 2NO3−(aq) + Cu(OH)2(s) → 2H2O(ℓ) + Cu^2+(aq) + 2NO3−(aq). Only NO3− appears unchanged on both sides.

prompt: Hydriodic acid, HI(aq), reacts with solid lead(II) hydroxide, Pb(OH)2(s). According to the solubility rules, which ions are spectator ions in this reaction?

choices.why: I− would be a spectator if the salt dissolved, but Pb^2+ is an exception to the iodide rule. PbI2 is insoluble, so the I− ions end up in the solid.
Pb^2+ is never a dissolved ion here: it starts in solid Pb(OH)2 and ends in solid PbI2.
H+ combines with OH− to form water, and I− ends up in solid PbI2, so neither is a spectator.

explanation: Pb(OH)2 is insoluble, and so is the salt PbI2, because Pb^2+ is an exception to the rule that iodides are soluble. The complete ionic equation is 2H+(aq) + 2I−(aq) + Pb(OH)2(s) → 2H2O(ℓ) + PbI2(s), and no ion appears unchanged on both sides.

prompt: Hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq), reacts with solid aluminum hydroxide, Al(OH)3(s), to form water and aluminum chloride. A student writes the net ionic equation as H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(ℓ). What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Al(OH)3 is insoluble, so it can't be split into ions and must appear as Al(OH)3(s)
The Cl− ions take part in the reaction, so they belong in the net ionic equation
choices.why: Cl− ions are dissolved on both sides and don't change, so they are spectator ions and are left out.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong, because every neutralization has this same net ionic equation
choices.why: H+ + OH− → H2O is the net ionic equation only when the base and salt are dissolved. An insoluble base stays together as a solid.

choices.text: The water should be written as separate H+(aq) and OH−(aq) ions on the product side
choices.why: Water is a product of the neutralization and is written as H2O(ℓ), not as separate ions.

explanation: Compounds of OH− are insoluble except those of Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+, NH4+, Sr^2+, and Ba^2+, so Al(OH)3 stays a solid. AlCl3 is soluble, so the net ionic equation is 3H+(aq) + Al(OH)3(s) → 3H2O(ℓ) + Al^3+(aq).

prompt: A solid acid reacts with a solid base to form water and an insoluble salt. How does the net ionic equation compare with the balanced chemical equation?

choices.text: They are the same, because nothing is dissolved that could be separated into ions
The net ionic equation is H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(ℓ), as for any neutralization
choices.why: That net ionic equation applies when the acid, base, and salt are dissolved. Solids can't be separated into ions, so they stay in the equation.

choices.text: No net ionic equation can be written, because no dissolved ions are present
choices.why: A net ionic equation can still be written. With nothing dissolved, it is simply the equation of the solids and the water.

choices.text: The net ionic equation shows only the salt, written as its separate ions
choices.why: The salt is insoluble, so it stays together as a solid with an (s) label rather than being split into ions.

explanation: Only dissolved ionic compounds are written as separate ions. When the acid, base, and salt are all solids, there is nothing to separate and no spectator ions to cancel, so the net ionic equation is the balanced equation itself.

prompt: Solutions of potassium hydroxide, KOH, and nitric acid, HNO3, are mixed in exactly the amounts needed to neutralize each other. Besides water, what does the final solution contain?

choices.why: H+ and OH− combine to form water in the neutralization, so they are used up.

choices.text: Solid KNO3 that settles to the bottom
choices.why: All compounds of K+ and all compounds of NO3− are soluble, so KNO3 stays dissolved as separate ions.

choices.text: Nothing else; it is pure water
choices.why: K+ and NO3− are spectator ions. They don't react, but they are still present in the solution.

explanation: The H+ from HNO3 and the OH− from KOH combine to form water. K+ and NO3− are spectator ions: they take no part in the reaction, but they remain dissolved, so the solution holds the salt KNO3 as separate ions.
